query: Our authentication backend uses jsonwebtoken@8.5.1 from auth0/node-jsonwebtoken with a configurable key retrieval callback. Are there known vulnerabilities? Explain whether they apply to our implementation.
answer:
Target:   auth0/node-jsonwebtoken @ b924272 · jsonwebtoken@8.5.1 · checked 2026-11-21
Decision: 🔴 Do not adopt

Yes, jsonwebtoken 8.5.1 has four known vulnerabilities, two high and two moderate, all fixed in
9.0.0. The key retrieval flaw is directly relevant to your design, so upgrade and fix the allowed
algorithms. Whether you can be attacked today depends on your callback and options, which I could
not see.

Why
 🟢 Licence: MIT licence, permissive and fine for business use.
   • LICENSE:1 The licence is MIT, which allows commercial use with a copyright notice.
     "The MIT License (MIT)" → https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/b924272f29192e12926b5414546f7c5bfcc9579d/LICENSE#L1 ✔
 🔴 Security: Four advisories affect 8.5.1; all fixed in 9.0.0. (CRA Art. 13(5))
   • Version 8.5.1 has a high vulnerability (GHSA-27h2-hvpr-p74q / CVE-2022-23529); fixed in 9.0.0.
     "jsonwebtoken has insecure input validation in jwt.verify function" → https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-27h2-hvpr-p74q ✔
   • Version 8.5.1 has a high vulnerability (GHSA-8cf7-32gw-wr33 / CVE-2022-23539); fixed in 9.0.0.
     "jsonwebtoken unrestricted key type could lead to legacy keys usage" → https://osv.dev/vulnerability/GHSA-8cf7-32gw-wr33 ✔
   🔴 8.5.1: high vulnerability GHSA-27h2-hvpr-p74q / CVE-2022-23529; fixed in 9.0.0

What to do next
 1. Upgrade jsonwebtoken to 9.0.0 or later; all four advisories list 9.0.0 as the fix. Test it,
   since 9.x is a major version.
 2. Always pass an explicit algorithms list to verify (for example ['RS256']), and never allow both
   shared-secret and public-key algorithms in the same callback.
 3. Make your key retrieval callback return only one key type and reject unknown key IDs; never
   build keys from token contents.

Limitations
 • Open question: Does your key retrieval callback ever return both shared secrets and public keys,
   or choose keys from token header fields?
 • Open question: Do your verify calls set an explicit algorithms option?

Also checked: maintenance 🟢 Not archived; last commit June 2026; 218… · Not checked: privacy, skills

report.question: Are there known vulnerabilities in jsonwebtoken@8.5.1, and do they apply to our implementation with a configurable key retrieval callback?
assumptions: Your key retrieval callback and verify options were not visible to me, so applicability is assessed from the advisories, not your code.
Repo code was read at the latest commit, not at 8.5.1, so it shows the fixed behaviour only.

licence.summary: MIT licence, permissive and fine for business use.

security.summary: Four advisories affect 8.5.1; all fixed in 9.0.0.

maintenance.summary: Not archived; last commit June 2026; 218 open issues.

privacy.summary: Not checked; not relevant to the vulnerability question.

skills.summary: Not an AI-agent skill; not applicable.

findings.claim: Most relevant to you: a known flaw in how a key retrieval callback is handled could let attackers forge tokens. It applies if your callback can return different key types (for example a shared secret and a public key) and you do not fix the allowed algorithms.
findings.evidence_quote: jsonwebtoken's insecure implementation of key retrieval function could lead to Forgeable Public/Private Tokens
findings.why: Your design uses exactly the feature this advisory targets (CVE-2022-23541, moderate).
findings.uncertainty: I could not see your callback or verify options, so I cannot confirm you are exploitable.

findings.claim: If you call verify without an explicit list of allowed algorithms, an attacker may be able to bypass signature checks.
findings.evidence_quote: jsonwebtoken vulnerable to signature validation bypass due to insecure default algorithm in jwt.verify()
findings.why: Affects all versions below 9.0.0 (CVE-2022-23540); depends on whether you set the algorithms option.
findings.uncertainty: Unknown whether your code sets the algorithms option.

findings.claim: A high-severity flaw lets unrestricted key types, including legacy ones, be used to check tokens. It applies if your callback can return keys of weak or unexpected types.
findings.evidence_quote: jsonwebtoken unrestricted key type could lead to legacy keys usage
findings.why: High severity (CVE-2022-23539) and affects every version up to 8.5.1.
findings.uncertainty: Depends on which keys your callback returns and whether you control them.

findings.claim: A fourth high-severity advisory covers weak input checking in verify. It matters mainly if untrusted data can reach the key or options passed to verify.
findings.evidence_quote: jsonwebtoken has insecure input validation in jwt.verify function
findings.why: CVE-2022-23529 is high severity and affects 8.5.1.
findings.uncertainty: Exploitability depends on how your code builds the key and options.

findings.claim: The latest code adds checks that the key type matches the token algorithm, which is the kind of fix these advisories needed. This confirms upgrading is worthwhile; it is not a view of 8.5.1.
findings.uncertainty: I did not read the 8.5.1 source.

findings.claim: The licence is MIT, which allows commercial use with a copyright notice.

conditions: Upgrade jsonwebtoken to 9.0.0 or later; all four advisories list 9.0.0 as the fix. Test it, since 9.x is a major version.
Always pass an explicit algorithms list to verify (for example ['RS256']), and never allow both shared-secret and public-key algorithms in the same callback.
Make your key retrieval callback return only one key type and reject unknown key IDs; never build keys from token contents.
Until you upgrade, check logs for tokens with unexpected algorithm headers and consider rotating signing keys if you suspect abuse.
open_questions: Does your key retrieval callback ever return both shared secrets and public keys, or choose keys from token header fields?
Do your verify calls set an explicit algorithms option?

The key retrieval flaw is directly relevant to your design, so upgrade and fix the allowed algorithms. Whether you can be attacked today depends on your callback and options, which I could not see.
